celib.introTexte: Twenty questions about your daily life, your encounters and what goes on in your head. Two of them change depending on your answers. Answer the way things are, not the way you wish they were: nobody sees your answers.
celib.resultatLibelle: What holds you back the most
celib.q1: In a normal week, how many new people do you meet, to the point of exchanging at least a few words?
celib.q1a: Several, between work, an activity and friends.
celib.q1b: One or two, when a chance comes up.
celib.q1c: Almost none: I always see the same faces.
celib.q1d: None. Work, home, screen, and again the next day.
celib.q2a: Out and about, with people: colleagues, clients, a class, a sport.
celib.q2b: Between work and home, with outings at the weekend.
celib.q2c: Alone most of the time, working from home or at home, and I don't go out much.
celib.q2d: In a rhythm so full there is no room left for anything else.
celib.q3: Have you ever been in a relationship?
celib.q3a: No, never, or nothing I would call a relationship.
celib.q3b: Yes, but it was a long time ago.
celib.q3c: Yes, and it ended less than two years ago.
celib.q4: In your view, what made it never happen?
celib.q4b: Me: I don't dare, I let it pass, I never make a move.
celib.q4c: I don't think I'm attractive, so I don't really try.
celib.q4d: I haven't felt the need so far.
celib.q5: When you think back to your last relationship…
celib.q5a: It's behind me, I can talk about it without it stirring anything.
celib.q5b: It left marks, but I've moved on.
celib.q5c: I still compare, or I keep an eye on what they're up to.
celib.q5d: It hurt so much that I don't want to live through that again.
celib.q6a: Full: friends, invitations, new people through them.
celib.q6b: Decent: a small, loyal circle I see regularly.
celib.q6c: Reduced: a few friends I rarely see, almost all of them in couples.
celib.q6d: Almost at a standstill: I hardly go out anymore, and nobody invites me.
celib.q7: You like someone at a party or in a class. What happens?
celib.q7a: I find a way to go and talk to them, even clumsily.
celib.q7b: I wait for a sign from them, and if nothing comes, I let it go.
celib.q7c: I think about what I could say, and the moment passes.
celib.q7d: I assume they're not interested in me, so I don't even try.
celib.q8a: A tool I use, with real dates coming out of it.
celib.q8b: Installed, but I rarely open them and reply even less.
celib.q8c: I tried, I stopped: too many disappointments.
celib.q8d: Never installed, they're not for me.
celib.q9: On the apps, how does it usually go?
celib.q9a: Matches, conversations, and quite often a date.
celib.q9b: I pass on almost everyone: nobody suits me.
celib.q9c: I chat, but I never suggest meeting up, and it fizzles out.
celib.q9d: Few matches, and that confirms to me that I'm not attractive.
celib.q10: Without apps, where could you meet someone today?
celib.q10a: I have ideas and I act on them: parties, activities, friends of friends.
celib.q10b: Through friends, but they're all in couples and don't invite anymore.
celib.q10c: Honestly, nowhere: my life doesn't put anyone in my path.
celib.q10d: I'm not really looking. If it's meant to happen, it will.
celib.q11: You like someone, but they don't tick one of your important boxes: looks, job, age, city…
celib.q11a: I give it a chance, the box can wait.
celib.q11b: I hesitate, but I agree to see.
celib.q11c: I keep chatting, without believing in it.
celib.q11d: I stop there, I know what I want.
celib.q12: Someone you like shows interest in you. Your first thought?
celib.q12a: Great, let's see where it goes.
celib.q12b: Pleased, with a small twinge of doubt.
celib.q12d: There must be a misunderstanding, it can't be anything else.
celib.q13: If you met someone tomorrow, how much room would they have in your weeks?
celib.q13b: Room to be made, I'd have to adjust a little.
celib.q13c: Little room: work, sport and projects take up everything.
celib.q13d: I don't know, I've never really pictured it.
celib.q14a: I get back in touch, or reply quickly, and we see each other again.
celib.q14b: I wait for the other person to write, so as not to seem too keen.
celib.q14c: I go over everything that wasn't right, and I don't follow up.
celib.q14d: That doesn't happen to me: I haven't had a first date in a long time.
celib.q15: A relationship starts well. After a few weeks, it gets serious.
celib.q15a: That's what I'm looking for, it makes me happy.
celib.q15b: I'm pleased, but I slow down a little.
celib.q15c: I see flaws I didn't see before, and I pull away.
celib.q15d: I have no idea: I've never got past the first few weeks.
celib.q16: Talking to a stranger, in a queue, a class or at a party…
celib.q16b: Depends on the day, but I can do it.
celib.q16c: Stresses me out, I do everything to avoid it.
celib.q16d: Exhausts me in advance, so I avoid the places where it could happen.
celib.q17: What you expect from meeting someone…
celib.q17a: Someone things are simple with, the rest gets built.
celib.q17b: Something obvious fairly quickly, otherwise I doubt.
celib.q17c: Love at first sight, otherwise it's not the right person.
celib.q17d: Someone who will never hurt me.
celib.q18: When you talk about yourself to someone you like…
celib.q18a: I talk about myself simply, with my qualities and my flaws.
celib.q18b: I play it down, I don't want to sound like I'm boasting.
celib.q18c: I quickly point out my flaws, as if to warn them.
celib.q18d: I avoid talking about myself, I ask questions to fill the gaps.
celib.q19: Being in a relationship, today, is…
celib.q19a: A clear wish, I think about it often.
celib.q19b: A wish, but not to the point of changing my habits.
celib.q19c: A nice, distant idea, my life is already full.
celib.q19d: An almost painful need, I feel like I'm running late.
celib.q20a: Introduce me to people, take me to parties.
celib.q20b: Are there, but we always meet in the same setting.
celib.q20c: Are almost all in couples, with children, and we rarely see each other.
celib.q20d: Can be counted on one hand, and we mostly talk by message.
celib.q21: When a conversation starts with someone you like, by message or in person…
celib.q21a: It moves naturally towards a date.
celib.q21b: I reply late or little, and it fizzles out.
celib.q21c: I get carried away very fast, and the other person backs off.
celib.q21d: I test the other person, I look for the detail that's wrong.
celib.q22: When you ask yourself why you're single, the answer that comes to mind…
celib.q22a: I don't meet anyone, it's a matter of chances.
celib.q22b: I'm afraid: of approaching, of committing, of getting hurt.
celib.q22c: I'm too picky, or I'm waiting for perfection.
celib.q22d: There's something about me that doesn't work.
celib.p_occasions_t: You no longer meet anyone new
celib.p_occasions_d: Your answers describe a life that runs fine, but in a closed loop. Work, home, the same friends, the same places. Nothing wrong with that, except that encounters don't happen in a vacuum: they need new faces, and ideally the same new faces several times in a row. It's not you that's blocking things. It's your week that leaves chance no opening. Most couples formed where people see each other again: at university, at work, in an activity, in a circle of friends. When those places close, being single settles in without you having done anything wrong.
celib.p_occasions_a: Add one regular fixture to your week, not one more night out: a class, an association, a team sport, a place where you'll see the same people for several weeks. Repetition is what creates encounters, not the number of outings. And if your friends no longer invite, do the inviting yourself, asking each of them to bring along someone you don't know.
celib.p_occasions_c: your daily life hardly puts any new people in your path anymore, and that weighs on everything else.
celib.p_social_t: Your social life is running slow
celib.p_social_d: The circle has shrunk, often without you deciding it. Friends got into relationships, had children, moved away. Invitations became rarer, and you didn't necessarily pick up the slack. The result: fewer evenings out, fewer new people, and a habit of solitude that ends up being comfortable. The problem isn't that you're unattractive. It's that you're almost never in the places where an encounter could happen, and the social muscle, when it stops working, wastes away a little.
celib.p_social_a: Start small again: a message to a friend you've lost touch with, a "yes" to the next invitation, even without feeling like it. Then a group activity that comes round every week. The goal isn't to meet love straight away, it's to put people back into your life. Romantic encounters almost always come indirectly, through friends of friends.
celib.p_social_c: your circle has shrunk, and the chances to meet someone with it.
celib.p_aborder_t: You don't dare to make the first move
celib.p_aborder_d: You meet people, some of them you like, and that's where it stops. You wait for a sign, you look for the right line, you tell yourself it's not the moment. The moment passes. It's not shyness in the usual sense: it's the fear of being rejected, which weighs more than the wish to find out. Many people in your situation are very much at ease with their friends and only freeze when something is at stake. The result is the same: the stories that could have started don't start, and you walk away telling yourself it wouldn't have worked anyway.
celib.p_aborder_a: Practise in situations where nothing is at stake: asking for directions, making a remark to someone in a queue, saying hello to a neighbour. The point is to get your body used to the idea that talking to a stranger does nothing terrible. Then set yourself a simple rule: when you like someone, you say one sentence, any sentence, within three minutes. Not to seduce. Just so the moment doesn't pass.
celib.p_aborder_c: when you like someone, the fear of being rejected often wins over the wish to go and talk to them.
celib.p_passe_d: You can have been single for months and not be available. Your answers show it: a past relationship still taking up room, or a fear of getting hurt that makes you pull back as soon as things get serious. The two look alike from the outside. You meet someone, it goes well, then you find flaws, you slow down, you drift away. It isn't boredom, it's protection. It was useful once. Today, it costs you the stories that could have mattered.
celib.p_passe_a: Don't force the next encounter, it would only add a disappointment. First look at what is taking up the room. If it's an ex, cut what's left: social media, news through friends, the "just checking how you are" messages. If it's fear, put a name on the way you attach to people, and the next time the urge to leave comes, stay one more week to see what happens.
celib.p_passe_c: a part of you is still protecting itself, because of the past or for fear of getting hurt.
celib.p_filtre_t: Your filter lets too few people through
celib.p_filtre_d: You know what you want, and that's a quality. But your answers show a very quick sorting: a missing box, a first date without a spark, a detail that's off, and the person is set aside. At that rate, almost nobody gets through. The love at first sight you're waiting for exists, but it's rare, and many solid couples started with "not bad, worth seeing again". There's often something else behind a very precise list, by the way: it describes an ex, or an ideal version of yourself, and it also serves to take no risk at all.
celib.p_filtre_a: Try the experiment once: accept a second date with someone who didn't have an immediate effect on you but who you had a pleasant time with. Not to force yourself, to check. And reread your list of criteria asking yourself, for each one: could I be happy with someone who doesn't have it? The ones that remain are the real ones.
celib.p_filtre_c: you rule people out fast, and people who could have suited you don't make it past the first sorting.
celib.p_estime_t: You start out defeated before you've even tried
celib.p_estime_d: When someone shows interest in you, your first thought is that they'll be disappointed. So you don't go, or you go while apologising for being there. You play down what you're worth, you point out your flaws before anyone sees them, and you read the slightest silence as a confirmation. It's not about looks or qualities: it's the way you see yourself, and it shows. It makes you less available, it makes the other person doubt, and it ends up producing exactly what it feared.
celib.p_estime_a: Let the other person decide whether they're disappointed or not: it's not your job to do it for them. Concretely, the next time someone pays you a compliment, say thank you and nothing else. And for two weeks, note the moments when someone sought out your company. You'll see there are more than you think. If this view of yourself is old and heavy, talking to a professional about it is nothing excessive.
celib.p_estime_c: you doubt what you're worth, and that doubt makes you pull back or sabotage yourself.
celib.p_priorite_t: A relationship has no room in your current life
celib.p_priorite_d: You say you want a relationship, and it's probably true. But your answers show a life that's already full and organised, where someone else would have nowhere to fit. Work, sport, projects and habits take up everything. It isn't a flaw: it's a choice, often an unspoken one. The problem is the gap between the wish you state and the room there actually is. As long as it exists, encounters stay at the stage of a nice idea, and the people you meet quickly sense they would come after everything else.
celib.p_priorite_a: Decide, honestly. If a relationship is a real wish, make room for it before the encounter: one free evening a week, not filled in advance, and an activity where you see people. If you're fine as you are for now, say so to yourself clearly, it will spare you feeling like a failure at something you're not really looking for.
celib.p_priorite_c: your life is already full, and a relationship wouldn't have much room to slip into it.
celib.p_suite_t: Beginnings don't turn into a story
celib.p_suite_d: In your case, encounters happen. What sticks is what comes after: the first date with no follow-up, the conversation that fizzles out, the story that stops after three weeks. Often because the pace isn't right. Too fast, and the other person backs off. Too slow, and they conclude you're not interested. Or because you wait for the other person to do everything, or you look for the detail that's wrong from the second message. It isn't the encounter you need to work on, it's the way you let it grow.
celib.p_suite_a: After a good date, write the next day, simply, without calculating: "I had a good time, shall we do it again?". Don't make them guess your interest, say it. And if you tend to get carried away, keep your normal rhythm of life for the first few weeks: friends, sport, sleep. A story that's starting needs air on both sides.
celib.p_suite_c: you do meet people, but the first exchanges or the first dates don't lead anywhere.
celib.p_ouvert_t: Nothing is blocking you, what's mostly missing is time and chances
celib.p_ouvert_d: Your answers describe someone who is available: you dare to talk to people, you give things a chance, you don't run away when it gets serious and you don't put yourself down. None of the eight causes this test measures stands out. That means one simple thing: your being single has no deep reason. It comes down to the encounter that hasn't happened yet, and that is the easiest situation to shift. There's nothing to fix, only chances to multiply.
celib.p_ouvert_a: Carry on as you are, and add regularity: an activity where you see the same people again, a party where you don't know everyone, a yes to an invitation you would have declined. If you want to dig into what happens once you like someone, what holds you back at the moment of meeting is the next step.
